newsitem.title: USA: Dumping case among options U.S. studying for Canadian wheat.
newsitem.headline: Dumping case among options U.S. studying for Canadian wheat.

text.p: The United States is looking at options for curbing wheat imports from Canada, including a possible probe into whether Canada is dumping discounted wheat in the U.S. market, Clinton Administration officials said Thursday.
Canada responded swiftly, saying it was not dumping wheat and that U.S. complaints were unfounded.

"Three investigations have proven before that we're not doing that, we're not doing anything different than before, so there's no cause for anyone to even use the word dumping," Canadian Agriculture Minister Lyle Vanclief said in Ottawa.

Northern state senators and congressmen have long complained that Canadian wheat imports unfairly push down prices for U.S. wheat producers along the border. A group of northern lawmakers, who have demanded a halt to all Canadian wheat imports, met for nearly 90 minutes on Thursday with U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.
Glickman, speaking with reporters after the meeting, said "the level of concern is very high in the administration" about the recent increase in wheat imports from Canada.

"We're looking at options right now" for reducing the level of imports, Glickman said. However, he said no decision on any course of action had been made in the nearly 90-minute-long meeting with the lawmakers.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said the United States is also concerned about the amount of market access that Canada provides for U.S. wheat imports.

In the fall of 1994 the United States imposed a one-year, 1.5 million tonne quota on imports of wheat from Canada. However, Barshefsky acknowledged that there was "no current agreement" that limits the amount of wheat coming into the United States from Canada.
U.S. imports from Canada rose to 2.0 million tonnes for the wheat marketing year that ended May 31, according to the USDA.

"The Commerce Department is going to look at the issue of dumping," Barshefsky said, adding that the agency would soon meet with U.S. wheat producers to determine if a dumping investigation is warranted.
Canada has repeatedly said it did not expect shipments to U.S. buyers to top 1.5 million tonnes, but that it refused to recognise any constraint on its sales.

An aide at the Canadian Embassy in Washington estimated Canadian wheat shipments to the United States during Canada's 1996/97 marketing year, which ends Thursday, at about 1.5 million tonnes. That excludes shipments from Ontario since such shipments were exempted from the 1994/95 quota, he said.
Canada will not tolerate any attempt by the United States to restrict Canadian shipments and will probably take the case to the World Trade Organisation if necessary, the aide said.

North Dakota Senators Byron Dorgan and Kent Conrad, both Democrats, said their concern about wheat imports made them sceptical about the Clinton Administration's desire for so-called "fast track" negotiating authority to expand the North American Free Trade Agreement to include Chile.
Grain prices for U.S. wheat farmers in the Dakotas have plunged more than 30 percent since last year because of the Canadian imports, the lawmakers said.
"The injury to North Dakota is in the hundreds of millions of dollars," Conrad said. "We've got farmers going broke."
